title: Ezra 4:17–24
context: Artaxerxes replies to Rehum, Shimshai, and their companions (4:17–22). He reports that a search of the records found Jerusalem to have rebelled against kings in the past, that mighty kings once ruled from Jerusalem over the country beyond the River, and he orders the work stopped until a decree is made by him. Many readers think of David and Solomon in 4:20, though the letter names no one. When the reply is read, the opponents go to Jerusalem and stop the Jews by force (4:23). Then 4:24 states that work on God’s house stopped until the second year of Darius king of Persia. Many readers take 4:24 as resuming the thread of 4:5 after the survey of later opposition in 4:6–23, since it returns to the temple and to Darius, whose second year is also named in Haggai 1:1, Zechariah 1:1, and the resumption in Ezra 5:1–2; others relate the verses differently. The reply leaves room for a later decree, and Nehemiah 2:1–8 later presents a king named Artaxerxes granting Nehemiah leave to rebuild the city; this commentary names that notice without harmonizing the two. Both traditions read the forced halt soberly and see God’s providence at work through delay and opposition.

verses.text: Then the king sent an answer to Rehum the chancellor, and to Shimshai the scribe, and to the rest of their companions who live in Samaria, and in the rest of the country beyond the River: Peace.
verses.arminianNotes: The king answers Rehum, Shimshai, and their companions in Samaria and beyond the River with a greeting of peace. Arminian readers note that the opponents receive a hearing at the highest level, and they observe that the outcome for the returned community now depends, as far as human eyes can see, on an imperial decision beyond its control.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the king’s reply as one more step in a history God governs, since the king’s heart is in the LORD’s hand (Proverbs 21:1) even when his decision goes against God’s people for a time. Shared ground: both traditions read the exchange as showing the community’s vulnerability and both trust that God is not absent from imperial courts.

verses.text: The letter which you sent to us has been plainly read before me.
verses.arminianNotes: The king says the letter has been plainly read before him. Arminian readers note that a ruler forms his judgment from the information placed in front of him, which is why truthful reporting matters, and why believers are called to live so that accusations against them may be shown false over time.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the king hears only one side, yet God hears every side and will in time vindicate his work. Shared ground: both traditions read this verse as a reminder that human judgments, even by powerful rulers, are limited and dependent on what they are told, while God’s judgment is complete and just.

verses.text: I decreed, and search has been made, and it was found that this city has made insurrection against kings in the past, and that rebellion and revolts have been made in it.
verses.arminianNotes: The king reports that a search found the city had made insurrection against kings in the past. Arminian readers note that Israel’s past failures are brought up against a new generation, and they see in this the lasting consequences of earlier unfaithfulness that later believers must humbly bear while seeking to walk in a different way.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the records confirming what Scripture itself confesses, that Judah had rebelled (2 Chronicles 36:13), while also showing God’s mercy in restoring a people with such a history. Shared ground: both traditions read the king’s finding as accurate about the past but incomplete about God’s present purpose, and both see grace in the restoration of a people with a record of rebellion.

verses.text: There have also been mighty kings over Jerusalem who have ruled over all the country beyond the River; and tribute, custom, and toll was paid to them.
verses.arminianNotes: The king adds that mighty kings once ruled over Jerusalem and the whole country beyond the River and received tribute. Many readers think of the kingdom under David and Solomon, though the letter names no one. Arminian readers note the irony that Jerusalem’s former glory becomes a reason to fear and restrain it now.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in the memory of Jerusalem’s former kings a reminder of God’s promises to David, which no imperial decree could cancel. Shared ground: both traditions read the king’s words as an unwitting witness to Jerusalem’s past greatness under God’s blessing, and both see the promise to David as still standing beneath the setbacks of the present.

verses.text: Make a decree now to cause these men to cease, and that this city not be built until a decree is made by me.
verses.arminianNotes: The king orders the men to cease and the city not to be built until a decree is made by him. Arminian readers note that this decree is provisional, leaving room for a future decision, and they see in it how God’s people can be halted by legitimate authority for a time while their calling remains in place.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the phrase until a decree is made by me leaves the door open, and they see God already holding the future of the city in his hand even as the work is stopped. Shared ground: both traditions read the decree as a real setback, and both note that later Scripture records the city being rebuilt with royal permission (compare Nehemiah 2:5–8).

verses.text: Be careful that you not be slack doing so. Why should damage grow to the hurt of the kings?
verses.arminianNotes: The king warns his officials not to be slack, asking why damage should grow to the hurt of the kings. Arminian readers note how quickly a ruler acts when his interests appear threatened, and they draw a lesson about how believers can be caught between the concerns of the powerful and the calling of God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the king’s urgency as human power trying to secure itself, while the LORD remains sovereign over every throne and its anxieties. Shared ground: both traditions read the warning as showing the political pressure under which the returned community lived, and both affirm that no earthly power has the last word over God’s purposes.

verses.text: Then when the copy of King Artaxerxes’ letter was read before Rehum, Shimshai the scribe, and their companions, they went in haste to Jerusalem to the Jews, and made them to cease by force of arms.
verses.arminianNotes: When the king’s letter is read, the opponents go in haste to Jerusalem and make the Jews cease by force of arms. Arminian readers note that the halt is real and painful, imposed by coercion, and that faithful people are not promised freedom from setbacks, only God’s presence and help within them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see even this forced stoppage as within God’s governance, though they do not call the coercion good, and they note that God brings the work forward again in his time. Shared ground: both traditions affirm that God is not the author of the opponents’ hostility, that the opponents are responsible for their actions, and that he works through and beyond such opposition.

verses.text: Then work stopped on God’s house which is at Jerusalem. It stopped until the second year of the reign of Darius king of Persia.
verses.arminianNotes: The work on God’s house stops until the second year of Darius. Arminian readers note that delay is not defeat, and that Haggai 1:1 and Zechariah 1:1 later show the LORD sending prophets in that very year to call the people back to the work, inviting a renewed and willing response.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the halt as a pause within God’s plan, followed by the stirring of the leaders and people under Haggai and Zechariah (Haggai 1:14; Ezra 5:1–2). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as many readers do, as returning to the temple story of 4:5, and both see God’s providence working through delay to bring his house to completion (Ezra 6:14–15).
